clinicalPearls: Microglia, the brain's resident innate immune and antigen-presenting cells, arise from primitive yolk-sac macrophages that seed the CNS before the blood-brain barrier forms and are sustained largely by self-renewal rather than by replenishment from the circulation; under some conditions peripherally derived macrophages can become microglia-like and replace damaged cells.

Microglia sculpt and prune synapses via classical complement proteins (C1q, C3) and complement receptors; in Alzheimer's disease, excess beta-amyloid drives C1q/C3 tagging of synapses that are then eliminated by CR3-expressing microglia, and knockout of C1q or C3 can rescue some neurodegenerative pathology in models.

Genetic data link innate immunity to neurodegeneration: more than half of genes implicated in Alzheimer's GWAS involve innate immune/microglial processes, and loss-of-function mutations in the microglial receptor TREM2 increase Alzheimer's risk up to roughly fourfold.

Around 10% of frontotemporal degeneration cases are due to heterozygous granulin (GRN) mutations causing progranulin haploinsufficiency; progranulin is a neurotrophic factor essential for lysosomal function and microglial homeostasis.

Activated microglia (via IL-1alpha, TNF, and C1q) can convert astrocytes to a reactive, neurotoxic (A1) phenotype that loses phagocytic capacity and damages neurons and oligodendrocytes through complement, nitric oxide, and free radicals; astrocytes are non-cell-autonomous contributors across MS, AD, PD, and ALS.

The glymphatic system uses periarterial CSF inflow through aquaporin-4-rich astrocyte foot processes to clear interstitial solutes and debris; clearance accelerates during sleep, and in models sleep deprivation increased beta-amyloid plaque accumulation while aquaporin-4 knockout reduced interstitial flow.

Harrison proposes a prion-based reclassification of neurodegenerative disease in which host proteins (PrP, Abeta, tau, alpha-synuclein, SOD1, possibly huntingtin) adopt self-propagating, beta-sheet-rich conformations that template normal precursor protein and spread between synaptically connected neurons.

The prion concept holds that the transmissible agents of kuru, CJD, scrapie, and BSE are devoid of nucleic acid and composed of host-encoded protein; AD is framed as a 'double-prion' disease in which both Abeta and tau prions coexist.

Late onset of inherited neurodegenerations, despite lifelong expression of the mutant protein, is attributed to age-dependent decline in protein quality-control/clearance mechanisms, consistent with the view that these are disorders of the aging nervous system.

Toxic small oligomers, rather than the mature plaques, tangles, and inclusion bodies, are increasingly viewed as the harmful species; visible aggregates may represent a relatively protective sequestration of toxic protein.

Impaired autophagy and lysosomal handling are central to neurodegeneration; GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations underlie about 5% of Parkinson's disease and 8-9% of dementia with Lewy bodies, with bidirectional inhibition between alpha-synuclein and glucocerebrosidase.

Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and 3D cerebral organoids model human neurodevelopmental disease (microcephaly, lissencephaly/Miller-Dieker, fragile X, Rett, Timothy syndrome) and confirmed Zika virus tropism for human neural progenitor (radial glia) cells as the cause of congenital microcephaly.
harrison.pathophysiology: This foundational chapter frames nervous-system disease around several converging mechanisms rather than a single illness. (1) Neuroimmunology/neuroinflammation: microglia and brain macrophages (yolk-sac-derived innate immune cells) and astrocytes are active, non-passive participants that prune synapses through complement, present antigen, secrete cytokines and trophic factors, and can shift between homeostatic and tissue-damaging states; crosstalk among microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes produces non-cell-autonomous pathology in MS, AD, PD, and ALS. (2) Myelin biology: oligodendrocytes maintain saltatory conduction and provide metabolic/neuroprotective support to axons, with activity-dependent (adaptive) myelination. (3) Waste clearance: the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic-like vessels clear interstitial solutes and aggregated proteins, with sleep-dependent and age-dependent modulation via aquaporin-4. (4) The microbiome can influence brain disease through molecular mimicry, immune modulation, circulating bacterial metabolites, enteric neural signaling, and possible prion-like seeding (e.g., the unproven hypothesis that E. coli Curli templates alpha-synuclein). (5) Protein aggregation and prion biology: misfolded, self-propagating proteins (Abeta, tau, alpha-synuclein, PrP, SOD1, TDP-43, expanded-polyglutamine huntingtin) spread trans-synaptically; toxic oligomers, defective ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosome clearance, mitochondrial dynamics (fission/fusion via Drp1, MFN1/2, OPA1; mitophagy via PINK1/parkin), and retromer (VPS35/VPS26/VPS29) dysfunction all contribute to neuronal death. (6) Stem cell biology: iPSCs and cerebral organoids reproduce early human brain-development disorders and enable disease modeling and drug screening.

harrison.prognosis: As a mechanistic overview the chapter does not give a single prognosis. It frames many neurodegenerative diseases as relentlessly progressive disorders of the aging nervous system driven by self-propagating prion-like proteins, while emphasizing that emerging understanding of complement, microglial, lysosomal/autophagy, mitochondrial, and prion-clearance pathways offers new and rational therapeutic targets (e.g., anti-C1q and anti-TREM2 antibody trials, progranulin-directed and gene/protein-replacement strategies) and new hope for prevention, treatment, and repair.
pitfalls: Assuming that macroscopic aggregates (plaques, tangles, inclusion bodies) directly cause neuronal dysfunction; toxic soluble oligomers may be the harmful species and sequestration may be protective.
Viewing microglia and astrocytes as merely secondary scavengers; genetic evidence places them as primary drivers of many neurodegenerative conditions.
Treating the resting-versus-activated microglial dichotomy as adequate; single-cell data reveal extensive, functionally heterogeneous states.

Over-extrapolating from rodent models; several human organoid findings (e.g., outer radial glia defects in Miller-Dieker syndrome) were not seen in mice, and some iPSC findings require replication before confidence.
Accepting unproven microbiome-seeding hypotheses (e.g., bacterial Curli triggering Parkinson's) as established; no proven microbiome-modulating therapy yet exists for any brain disease.
Therapeutic targeting of broadly acting systems (e.g., complement) risks off-target toxicity and loss of homeostatic functions such as physiologic synaptic pruning.
management: Direct disease-modifying therapy at the underlying molecular lesion where available, such as anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies that promote clearance of beta-amyloid in Alzheimer's disease
Target the innate-immune, complement-mediated synapse loss and reactive astrocyte pathways now recognised as drivers, an emerging focus of neuroinflammation-directed therapeutics
Provide symptomatic pharmacotherapy tailored to the syndrome, for example dopaminergic replacement in Parkinsonism and immunomodulation in multiple sclerosis
Optimise sleep and the glymphatic clearance that removes interstitial aggregates, and address modifiable factors that accelerate protein accumulation
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy for progressive motor and cognitive decline
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing for the heritable forms, including familial mutations in APP, MAPT, SOD1, C9orf72 and progranulin
Anticipate the relentlessly progressive course with advance care planning and palliative support
